This CLI tool's readme can be accessed via the root of the mlflow repository as follows: ```bash dev/dev-env-setup.sh -h ``` An example usage of this script that will build a development environment using `virtualenv` and the minimum supported Python version (to ensure compatibility) is: ```bash dev/dev-env-setup.sh -d .venvs/mlflow-dev -q ``` The `-q` parameter is to "quiet" the pip install processes preventing stdout printing during installation. It is advised to follow all of the prompts to ensure that the configuration of the environment, as well as git, are completed so that your PR process is as effortless as possible. **Note** Frequently, a specific version of a library is required in order to validate a feature's compatibility with older versions. Modifying your primary development environment to test one-off compatibility can be very error-prone and result in an environment that is significantly different from that of the CI test environment. To support this use case, the automated script can be used to create an environment that can be easily modified to support testing a particular version of a model flavor in an isolated environment. Simply run the `dev-env-setup.sh` script, activate the new environment, and install the required version for testing. Example of installing an older version of `scikit-learn` to perform isolated testing: ```bash dev/dev-env-setup.sh -d ~/.venvs/sklearn-test -q source ~/.venvs/sklearn-test/bin/activate pip freeze | grep "scikit-learn" >> scikit-learn==1.0.2 pip install scikit-learn==1.

    capture the input and output of the function. When it is applied to a method, it doesn't
    capture the `self` argument. Any exception raised within the function will set the span
    status to ``ERROR`` and detailed information such as exception message and stacktrace
    will be recorded to the ``attributes`` field of the span.

    For example, the following code will yield a span with the name ``"my_function"``,
    capturing the input arguments ``x`` and ``y``, and the output of the function.

    .. code-block:: python
        :test:

        import mlflow


        @mlflow.trace
        def my_function(x, y):
            return x + y

    This is equivalent to doing the following using the :py:func:`mlflow.start_span` context
    manager, but requires less boilerplate code.

    .. code-block:: python
        :test:

        import mlflow


        def my_function(x, y):
            return x + y


        with mlflow.start_span("my_function") as span:
            x = 1
            y = 2
            span.set_inputs({"x": x, "y": y})
            result = my_function(x, y)
            span.set_outputs({"output": result})

rows.title: [FR] Allow backend-resolved `UnityCatalog` locations in `mlflow.tracing.set_destination`
rows.excerpt:
merged 2026-03-06) added `UnityCatalog` handling to the registry, span processor, `get_active_spans_table_name` and, per its description, `set_destination`. The rejection was added during that PR's review in commit a76ce1de ("Disallow UnityCatalog in set_destination and env destination") without a recorded rationale in the PR thread, and #21385 ("Add trace location param to set_experiment", merged 2026-03-12) kept it while introducing the `set_experiment(trace_location=...)` flow. If either of you remembers the reasoning behind the rejection, I would be glad to hear it, since the rest of this section is my reconstruction from the code.

Reading the code, I believe the guard protects against a real failure mode, and this proposal keeps protecting against it: `UnityCatalog.full_otel_spans_table_name` simply returns `_otel_spans_table_name`, which is only populated by the backend (`TracingClient._create_or_get_trace_location`, `Experiment.trace_location` from experiment tags, `from_proto` / `from_dict`). A hand-built `UnityCatalog("catalog", "schema", "prefix")` therefore has no spans table name. If `set_destination` accepted it blindly, `_get_span_processors` would select the UC exporter and every export would then be silently skipped in `DatabricksUCTableSpanExporter._export_spans_incrementally` ("No active spans table name found. Skipping span export."). Pointing users at `set_experiment`, which provisions and links the tables, avoids that. The proposal below narrows the guard to exactly that case instead of rejecting the whole type.

**Proposed implementation** (all in `mlflow/tracing/provider.py` and `tests/tracing/test_provider.py`):

1. In `set_destination`, replace the blanket `isinstance(destination, UnityCatalog)` rejection with a rejection of *unresolved* locations only:

   ```python
   if isinstance(destination, UnityCatalog) and not destination.full_otel_spans_table_name:
       raise MlflowException.invalid_parameter_value(
           "The `UnityCatalog` destination does not carry the table names assigned by the "
           "Databricks backend, so traces cannot be exported to it. Pass a location resolved "
           "by the backend, e.g. `mlflow.set_experiment(..., "
           "trace_location=UnityCatalog(...)).trace_location` or "
           "`mlflow.get_experiment(experiment_id).trace_location`."
       )
   ```
